name: Yeke Kingdom (Garanganze)
summary: A trading kingdom in Katanga founded by the Nyamwezi trader Msiri, rich from copper, ivory and slaves; Msiri was killed by a Belgian-led expedition in 1891.

location.value: Southern Katanga in today’s DR Congo, centred on the capital Bunkeya near the Lufira River.

terrain.value: The high Katanga plateau with river valleys such as the Lufira, open woodland and copper-bearing hills.

climate.value: Tropical highland climate with a rainy season from about November to April and a cool dry season.

resources.value: Rich copper deposits worked into ingots and crosses, ivory from elephant hunting, salt and iron.

disasters.value: Droughts and famine are likely, made worse by the wars and revolts of the late 1880s.

population.value: Unknown; perhaps tens of thousands under direct rule, with more in tributary chiefdoms.

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages; a royal or market town.

migration.value: Nyamwezi traders and elephant hunters from today’s Tanzania, led by Msiri, settled among the Sanga in the 1850s.

economicBase.value: Long-distance trade in copper, ivory and enslaved people, plus tribute from local chiefs and farming.

tradeRoutes.value: Msiri traded Katanga’s copper principally, and also slaves and ivory, in return for gunpowder and firearms.

wealth.value: Msiri grew rich from trade and tribute, controlling copper and ivory that bought guns and cloth.

moneyAndTax.value: Tribute, cloth, cowries and trade goods.

inequality.value: Rulers and nobles above farmers; captives and slaves at the bottom.

governmentType.value: A monarchy built by Msiri, who ruled from Bunkeya through Yeke followers and subject chiefs.

keyRulers.value: Msiri (ruled about 1856–1891), the Nyamwezi trader who founded the kingdom and was killed in 1891.

succession.value: Effectively ended with Msiri’s death in 1891; his son Mukanda Bantu then ruled as a chief under the Congo Free State.

institutions.value: Rule through Yeke relatives and followers placed over local chiefs, who paid tribute to Bunkeya.

stability.value: Unstable by the late 1880s, when the Sanga and other subject peoples rose against Msiri’s rule.

eliteConflict.value: Conflict between the Yeke ruling group and subject peoples, above all the Sanga, who revolted in the late 1880s.

armyAndTech.value: Musket-armed fighters supplied by traders from both coasts, alongside spears and bows.

majorWars.value: Conquest of local chiefdoms; the Sanga revolt; and the Stairs Expedition, during which Msiri was shot in December 1891.

territoryChange.value: Expanded over southern Katanga and Kazembe’s western lands, then was absorbed into the Congo Free State in 1891.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals of the Lunda kingdom of Kazembe on the Luapula River and of Luba chiefdoms to the north.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; copper was cast into cross-shaped ingots used in trade.

scienceEducation.value: Oral learning; Qur’anic schools where Islam spread.

openness.value: Open to traders from both coasts and to missionaries such as Frederick Arnot, who reached Bunkeya in 1886.

communicationTransport.value: Footpaths walked by porter caravans carrying copper and ivory; canoes on rivers such as the Lufira.

religion.value: Traditional beliefs in ancestors and spirits; Christian missionaries arrived from 1886 but made few converts.

languageWriting.value: Kiyeke (related to Nyamwezi) among the rulers, local Sanga languages, and Swahili for trade; no local writing.

artsArchitecture.value: Thatched houses in large settlements at Bunkeya; copper and ironwork and carved objects.

socialStructure.value: A Yeke ruling group of Nyamwezi origin above local Sanga and other peoples, with captives and slaves at the bottom.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to Msiri and the Yeke ruling group rather than a shared identity with subject peoples.

dailyLife.value: Village farming; cassava, millet or sorghum.

neighbours.value: The Lunda kingdom of Kazembe, Luba chiefdoms, Sanga and Lamba peoples, and Swahili-Arab traders to the east.

ideasReligions.value: Traditional religion remained strong; Christianity reached Bunkeya with Plymouth Brethren missionaries from 1886.

colonisation.value: Taken over by King Leopold II’s Congo Free State after the Stairs Expedition killed Msiri in 1891.

riseSignals.value: The kingdom lasted about 1856 to 1891 under Msiri, a Nyamwezi from Tabora who became successor to a Wasanga chief and conquered neighbouring peoples; the capital was Bunkeya.

peakPeriod.value: The 1870s and early 1880s, when Bunkeya controlled the Katanga copper and ivory trade.

declineSignals.value: Revolts of subject peoples in the late 1880s and pressure from European expeditions.

outcome.value: The Stairs Expedition of Leopold II’s Congo Free State ended the kingdom by killing Msiri on 20 December 1891; his adopted son Mukanda-Bantu was installed over a small area of about 20 km radius around Bunkeya, and the title Mwata Msiri continues.

overallCertainty.value: Known from oral traditions, travellers and colonial records; many dates are approximate.
